text: Cyprus is an island in the Eastern Basin of the Mediterranean Sea, ranking as the third-largest island in the Mediterranean after Sicily and Sardinia and the 80th-largest island globally by area. It lies south of the Anatolian Peninsula and is part of the Cyprus Arc. Geographically, it is classified in West Asia, though it is considered a European country in political geography. The island has experienced prolonged periods of Greek influence, along with intermittent Anatolian, Levantine, Byzantine, Ottoman, and Western European influence. It is dominated by two mountain ranges—the Troodos Mountains and the Kyrenia Mountains (also known as Pentadaktylos)—with the central plain, the Mesaoria, lying between them. The Troodos Mountains cover about half the island and stretch from Pomos Point in the northwest to Larnaca Bay in the east, featuring a complex, fragmented structure with steep valleys and stepped foothills in the southwest. The Kyrenia Range, a narrow limestone ridge along the northern coast, rises suddenly from the plains and extends into the Karpas Peninsula, which points toward Asia Minor, reflecting Cyprus’s geological connection to that region. The Kyrenia Range is known for its jagged, Gothic-like peaks and is less than half the height of Mount Olympus (1,952 m or 6,404 ft), the highest point in Cyprus, which is located in the Troodos Mountains. The Kyrenia Range is also referred to as the Pentadactylon Mountains due to its five-fingered summit shape. Ancient copper deposits were found on the Troodos slopes, originating from massive sulphide deposits within an ophiolite complex formed at a spreading centre under the Mediterranean Sea and uplifted during the Pleistocene. Access to year-round water is difficult across much of the island, traditionally attributed to deforestation and erosion, though Grove and Rackham challenge this view; instead, winter rivers originate in the Troodos and flow in various directions, including the Yialias and Pedhieos rivers flowing eastward into Famagusta Bay and the Serraghis River flowing northwest through the Morphou plain, all of which dry up in summer. An extensive network of dams and waterways has been built to supply farming areas. The Mesaoria plain is the island’s agricultural heartland, with crop productivity depending heavily on winter rainfall, and other crops grown under irrigation. Historically, the island was richly forested, especially in the Troodos and Kyrenia ranges and in the Mesaoria, though ancient conquerors removed much of the timber for shipbuilding, leaving little evidence today. About 12% of the island is classified as woodland, with shrub communities like golden oak, strawberry tree, terebinth, olive, kermes oak, and styrax found in non-forested areas, though maquis is uncommon. Most untended land is covered by garrigue, composed of low bushes such as Cistus, Genista sphacelata, Calicotome villosa, Lithospermum hispidulum, Phagnalon rupestre, and locally Pistacia lentiscus; excessive grazing leads to impoverished batha with stunted herbs. The island has a Mediterranean climate with warm, dry summers (mid-May to mid-September) and mild, rainy winters (November to mid-March), with temperature and rainfall variations influenced by altitude and distance from the coast. The total area of Cyprus is 9,251 km², of which 5,896 km² are under the Republic of Cyprus and 3,355 km² under the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus; land area is 9,241 km² and water area is 10 km². The island has no land boundaries and a coastline of 648 km. Its maritime claims include a territorial sea of 12 nmi (22.2 km; 13.8 mi), a continental shelf extending to 200 m depth or to the depth of exploitation, and an exclusive economic zone of 98,707 km² (38,111 mi²). The elevation extremes are 0 m at sea level and 1,952 m at Mount Olympus. Natural resources include copper, pyrite, asbestos, gypsum, timber, salt, marble, and clay earth pigment. Land use in 2012 shows 9.90% arable land, 3.24% permanent crops, and 86.86% other land. Irrigated land was 457.9 km² in 2007, and total renewable water resources were 0.78 km³ in 2011. Freshwater withdrawal in 2009 was 0.18 km³ per year (10% domestic, 3% industrial, 86% agricultural), with a per capita rate of 164.7 m³/year. Natural hazards include moderate earthquake activity and droughts. Current environmental issues involve water resource problems due to the lack of natural reservoirs, seasonal rainfall disparities, seawater intrusion into the island’s largest aquifer, increased salinization in the north, water pollution from sewage and industrial waste, coastal degradation, and loss of wildlife habitats from urbanization. Cyprus is a party to international environmental agreements including Air Pollution, Air Pollution-Persistent Organic Pollutants, Biodiversity, Climate Change, Climate Change-Kyoto Protocol, Endangered Species, Environmental Modification, Hazardous Wastes, Law of the Sea, Marine Dumping, Nuclear Test Ban, Ozone Layer Protection, Ship Pollution, and Wetlands, with no signed but unratified agreements.
